title: AP CSP — Lesson 20 Homework: Searching & Comparing Algorithms
notice: All questions are original. Q1–Q6 are AP-style practice, not official or past AP questions; Q7–Q12 are classroom written practice, not official FRQs. These 30 marks are teacher-assigned, not AP exam scoring. Select exactly TWO answers in Q5; its one mark requires both correct choices and no others. All inputs are valid unless stated. DISPLAY outputs values in execution order. Show reasoning; braces and indentation identify each block.

questions.explanation: A uses AP one-based indexing. B uses a zero-based interpretation. C selects the last element. D returns the index rather than the stored value.

questions.prompt: Which property allows an ascending binary search to discard all values left of a midpoint when the target is greater than that midpoint?

options.label: B
options.text: The list is sorted in ascending order.

questions.explanation: B guarantees that the left values are no larger than the midpoint. Positivity and odd length are not prerequisites. A target may be absent; binary search must still conclude not found.

questions.prompt: An early-stopping linear search checks [3,8,12,19,27,34,50] from the beginning for target 34. How many elements are checked?
questions.explanation: C counts 3,8,12,19,27,34. A matches binary search for this target. B stops before examining the match. D unnecessarily examines the last element after finding it.

questions.prompt: Binary search checks the middle value 19 in [3,8,12,19,27,34,50] for target 34. Which candidates remain?
questions.explanation: D keeps values strictly above the checked 19. A keeps the wrong half. B retains an already ruled-out midpoint. C assumes the answer before inspecting the next midpoint.

questions.prompt: Which TWO statements are correct? Select exactly TWO.

options.label: B
options.text: Binary search can conclude that a target is absent.

options.label: C
options.text: Different correct searches can return the same membership result with different costs.

options.label: D
options.text: Binary search always uses fewer checks than linear search for every target.

questions.explanation: B stops after all candidates are eliminated. C separates correctness from cost. A is false because linear search can inspect unsorted data. D fails when the target is the first element of the list. Award one mark only for B and C together.

questions.prompt: A sorted list has 31 distinct elements. Binary search checks one midpoint at each step. The possible interval sizes before checks are 31,15,7,3,1. What is the maximum number of checks?
questions.explanation: B counts the five nonempty intervals. A counts gaps between them instead of checks. C is the size after one elimination. D is the linear-search maximum.

questions.prompt: Search [3,8,12,19,27,34,50] for 50 using binary search. Give each inspected value in order and the total number of element checks.
questions.explanation: Each comparison retains the larger-valued side until the last remaining candidate matches.

rubric.criterion: Gives first inspected value 19.
Gives second inspected value 34.
Gives third inspected value 50.
Gives three element checks.

questions.prompt: Search [3,8,12,19,27,34,50] for 28 using binary search. Give the three inspected values and explain why the final result is false.
questions.answer: 19 → 34 → 27; false because after ruling out 27 no candidate remains.
questions.explanation: 28 is above 19 but below 34, leaving only 27, which is not equal to 28.

rubric.criterion: Gives first inspected value 19.
Gives second inspected value 34.
Gives third inspected value 27.
Explains that all candidates are eliminated without a match, so the result is false.

questions.prompt: An incorrect search uses [9,1,7,3,5] for target 9. It checks the middle value 7, then keeps only the values to its right because 9 > 7. Identify the broken prerequisite, the remaining values, the lost target, and one valid repair.
questions.answer: The data are unsorted. Remaining values are 3 and 5. The target 9 was discarded on the left. Repair: sort first and apply binary search, or use linear search on the unsorted list.
questions.explanation: The value comparison alone cannot justify discarding the left half unless order relates that half to the midpoint.

rubric.criterion: Identifies the missing sorted-order prerequisite.
Gives remaining values 3 and 5.
Explains that the actual 9 on the left has been discarded.
Gives a valid repair: linear search directly or sort before binary search.

questions.prompt: For [3,8,12,19,27,34,50], compare early-stopping linear and binary search for target 3. State each count, whether the membership results agree, and why this disproves a claim that binary is faster on every individual input.
questions.answer: Linear: 1 check. Binary: 3 checks (19,8,3). Both return true. Linear checks fewer elements on this valid input, so the universal claim is false.
questions.explanation: Binary is often efficient on sorted data, but an individual target at the beginning favors linear search.

rubric.criterion: Gives linear count 1.
Gives binary count 3.
States that both return true for membership.
Uses this input as a counterexample to the claim that binary always takes fewer checks.

questions.prompt: Two algorithms answer whether a target is in a list. State when early-stopping linear search returns true, when it returns false, when binary search returns false, and what it means for their results to agree for the same valid input.
questions.answer: Linear returns true on a matching element; false after checking every element without a match. Binary returns false after no candidate remains without a match. Agreement means both return the same membership Boolean for that list and target.
questions.explanation: Matching results do not require matching sequences of inspected elements or matching costs.

rubric.criterion: States that a matching element makes linear search succeed.
States that checking the whole list without a match makes linear search fail.
States that exhausting binary candidates without a match makes binary search fail.
Defines agreement as the same true/false membership result for the same valid input.

questions.prompt: A student performs one search on an unsorted list today. Another application performs many searches on an already sorted list. Recommend a suitable method for each, give one reason for each recommendation, and address preparation cost.
questions.answer: One unsorted query: linear search is a simple valid choice because it requires no sorting. Many queries on already sorted data: binary search can reduce candidates by about half per step. Sorting has a cost if it is needed; compare preparation plus searches when choosing for unsorted data.
questions.explanation: These are justified choices, not a claim that one implementation is always faster for every size and target.

rubric.criterion: Recommends linear search as a suitable option for the one-time unsorted query.
Explains that linear search works without sorting or examines elements directly.
Recommends binary search for already sorted repeated queries and relates it to interval halving.
Acknowledges sorting/preparation cost when evaluating a strategy for initially unsorted data.
